cues.text: A Sharecropper's Son
Born Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli in 1881, he was the fourth of thirteen children in a family of sharecroppers near Bergamo, Italy.
He entered the seminary young and was ordained in 1904.

He spent much of his career in Vatican diplomatic service, serving as papal representative in Bulgaria, Greece, and Turkey, later as nuncio to France, and eventually becoming Patriarch of Venice and a cardinal in 1953.
Saving Lives During the War
During the Second World War, Roncalli served as apostolic delegate in Turkey and Greece.
He used his diplomatic position to help facilitate the rescue of a significant number of Jews from Nazi deportation and death.
He issued false baptismal certificates and transit documents that allowed many to escape occupied Europe.
An Unexpected Election

Elected pope in 1958 at nearly seventy-seven, Roncalli was widely expected by the cardinals who chose him to serve as a brief, uneventful 'interim' pontiff — a papa di passaggio — following the long, formal reign of Pius XII.
His warmth, humor, and evident personal simplicity quickly won him enormous popular affection, earning him the nickname 'Good Pope John.'
Convening Vatican II
Confounding expectations of a quiet caretaker papacy, John XXIII announced on January 25, 1959, his intention to convene an ecumenical council.
It became the Second Vatican Council , opened on October 11, 1962, the most consequential gathering of Catholic bishops in four centuries.
It was intended to bring the Church into renewed, more open engagement with the modern world.
A World Statesman
John XXIII also played a quiet mediating role during the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962, appealing publicly for restraint on both sides.
He did so at a moment of extreme nuclear tension and issued the influential encyclical Pacem in Terris in 1963.
It addressed world peace and human rights to believers and non-believers alike — a notably universal address for a papal document of its era.
Legacy
John XXIII died of stomach cancer in June 1963, less than five years into his papacy and before the Council he had convened could conclude — a task left to his successor, Paul VI .
Beatified in 2000 and canonized in 2014 by Pope Francis, he remains one of the most universally beloved popes of the modern era.
He is remembered for a papacy that, in his own words, sought above all 'to bring the Church up to date.'
